title: A Hundred Years After ‘La Cristiada’
author: Lorenzo Meyer
content:
_This article by[Lorenzo Meyer](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/lorenzo-
meyer) originally appeared in the [August 27, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4860145/a-cien-anos-de-la-cristiada/),
an independent Mexican digital news outlet._

As Carl von Clausewitz aptly observed, war is the continuation of politics by
other means. The Prussian soldier's definition is very much to the point when
reflecting on the centennial of one of our most bitter internal wars: the
Cristero war, or "cristiada," which today occupies barely a couple of pages in
school textbooks and six in the book published in 1979 by the Ministry of
Defense, _El ejército mexicano_ , a voluminous history in which the maps and
lists of towns barely left room for a very brief text where what really draws
attention, coming from where it does, is a kind of conclusion that accepts
that the Cristeros, "Mexicans after all, fought valiantly," against the
established Government.

The emergence, exactly one hundred years ago, of a popular anti-government
army in the center of the country invites a deeper reflection, for that
struggle (which cost the lives of tens of thousands of Mexicans, though we do
not know exactly how many) ultimately did not lead to any substantive
political change.

The clash between the Catholic Church and the revolutionary regime turned into
war precisely because the parties failed at what Clausewitz emphasized: the
period before hostilities, that is, the time of political negotiation. What
happened after the violent collision was simply the consolidation of the
status quo ante in the relationship between the regime and the Church, which
ended up institutionalizing a coexistence quite comfortable for both parties,
which leads one to ask whether the war served any purpose at all.

The conventional start of what became a new great civil war, just as the one
of the Mexican Revolution had barely ended, is usually dated to July 2, 1926,
when the "Calles Law" was published in the Official Gazette, a regulation of
Article 130 of the Constitution that hardened and narrowed the space and
manner in which churches (the Catholic one, in reality) could carry out their
professional activities. Of course, the start could also be dated a few days
later, on the 26th of that month, when the Catholic Church announced that, in
protest against the regulation imposed on it, it would close its temples and
suspend its services (masses, sacraments, etc.). In any case, by the end of
August the first armed clashes took place between government forces and groups
of Catholic civilians who would end up organizing themselves as the Cristero
army.

The confrontation had, by 1927–1928, become a substantial armed clash in which
the insurgent side sought, in the name of the defense of the Catholic
religion, to put an end to the revolutionary regime that was only just taking
shape. However, the root of such a great undertaking can be found much
earlier: in the difference and clash of the political projects that emerged
shortly after Mexico achieved its Independence. It was the clash of two
projects of Nation, the liberal and the conservative, which in the mid-
nineteenth century fought each other to the death but which, at the beginning
of the following century, seemed to have been definitively overcome as a
result of the triumph of liberal arms in 1867.

Nevertheless, the violence that, for religious motives, once again convulsed
our country while the aftermath of the Mexican Revolution was still being felt
can be better understood if it is seen as the reemergence of that tremendous
political and military clash that were the civil wars of the previous century.

That violence we know as the War of the Reform had as its central cause,
though not its only one, the effort of the liberal side to radically and
definitively separate the structures of the State from those of the Catholic
Church. The union of State and Church was one of the main features of the
three-century political system in New Spain, and the conservative project was
precisely to maintain that symbiosis, holding that in independent Mexico it
was the only way to give unity to a Nation built on a highly fragmented social
base. For the liberals of the time, on the contrary, freeing the State from
the influence of the Church was a sine qua non condition for making the
economy of the young country viable, beginning to put an end to the historical
fragmentation of its social base, and achieving a national identity beyond
religious beliefs.

The defeat of the original conservative project, sealed with the execution by
firing squad of Emperor Maximilian, did not mean, as would be seen in the
events of the 1920s, the resignation and adaptation of the Catholic hierarchy
to the new reality. The influence of the Catholic Church in the everyday life
of the country, above all in the worlds of rural and majority Mexico, was
dominant. Works such as _Pedro Páramo_ by Juan Rulfo and _Al filo del agua_ by
Agustín Yáñez, or microhistories such as _Pueblo en vilo_ by Luis González,
are so many windows that allow us to gauge the importance (not only religious
but political, cultural, and identity-related) of the Catholic Church in much
of central Mexico where, despite the changes introduced by the Revolution or
precisely because of them, it turned out to be fertile ground for the
resurgence of a violent reaction against a Government that, among other
things, remained bent on imposing the values of the secular State in spheres
that, in practice, the Church and the Catholic community still considered
their own.

The great work (more than a thousand pages) by Jean Meyer, _La Cristiada_ ,
published in Spanish in three volumes in 1973, shows that in its zone of
operations the Cristero army had a solid social base of support, multiclass
and highly motivated by the possibility of putting an end, not simply to the
anticlerical measures of President Calles's government, but, in the name of
Christ the King and the most holy Virgin of Guadalupe, to a regime they
supposed was determined to do away with the religion of the people. It is
worth noting that in that juncture, and although a good number of priests took
up arms, the Catholic Church as such did not choose to join the rebellion
openly. The federal Government, which in that period also had to confront an
old uprising with an Indigenous base (that of the Yaquis in Sonora) had an
army that was only just being organized and professionalized, but whose
command had serious internal divisions that would erupt later. In any case,
the head of the Government force, General Joaquín Amaro, concentrated his
troops in the states where the Cristero social base was strongest (Jalisco,
Michoacán, Guanajuato, Nayarit, Colima, Aguascalientes, Zacatecas, and
Durango) and arranged for a force of irregulars made up of agraristas, notably
from San Luis Potosí, to operate as auxiliaries of the regular army.

The composition of the contending sides (in a civil war that was particularly
brutal on both sides and where practically no prisoners were taken) turned out
to be very similar, since the federal soldiers and their agrarista auxiliaries
were also mostly Catholic and of peasant origin.

Unlike what occurred during the Revolution, the Cristero war had no great
decisive battles like, for example, the great battles of Zacatecas or Celaya a
few years earlier. The Cristeros always had difficulty arming themselves and
did not have the participation of professional military men, except for the
case of General Enrique Gorostieta, killed in action. By 1929 it was evident
that the Cristeros were not going to defeat the Government forces, but it was
equally clear that the Government could not put an end to its adversaries
quickly and decisively. Hence, with the mediation of the Washington Government
(which did not want more instability south of the Bravo), interim President
Emilio Portes Gil met with two bishops (Leopoldo Ruiz and Pascual Díaz) to
finally return to politics and declare, each side on its own, that the
Government did not intend to interfere with the religious beliefs of society
or to destroy the Catholic Church, and that the Church, in turn, did not
intend to disavow the authority of the Government and was making a call to the
rebels to lay down their arms.

On June 21, 1929, the church bells rang out to announce the return to
normality. But since the Cristero combatants themselves were not taken into
account in what were called "the arrangements" of '29, they did not consider
themselves defeated but rather betrayed by the Catholic hierarchy. Most of the
rebels laid down their arms, but not all. And to better understand those who
continued the fight until the end of the 1930s (in what has been called the
"Second Cristiada") one can turn to a moving autobiographical work: _Rescoldo.
Los últimos cristeros_ , by Antonio Estrada.

In 1934, General Lázaro Cárdenas took charge of the new regime; in 1936 the
former president and author of the "Calles Law" was expelled from the country
by Cárdenas; the Agrarian Reform gained strength and generated a large peasant
base of support for the regime of the Mexican Revolution. Nevertheless, the
embers of the war, of the "Second Cristiada," persisted throughout the second
half of the 1930s, although from 1940 on "la cristiada" began to become
history, part of our history as a nation.

And so, how are we to interpret today a conflict that cost the lives of, by
estimates ranging between 90,000 and 200,000 Mexicans? In practice the
government prevailed over its adversaries, and militant Catholics no longer
questioned the legitimacy or the reversibility of the secular State. The modus
vivendi reached in 1929 simply took root and, at the end of the last century,
in 1992, it was institutionalized with the government's recognition of the
churches as legitimate organizations with rights and obligations, and with the
establishment of diplomatic relations between the Mexican Government and the
Vatican.

Could this result have been reached without the political confrontation
turning into the war it became? It is very probable, for in the end that
painful struggle did not modify in any substantive way the legal framework in
which the secularism of the State operated; rather, it reaffirmed it. On the
other hand, the Catholicism of the bulk of Mexicans held firm, and if anything
changed in this last respect, it was more the product of the passage of time
and of social change than the result of specific Government policies.

In short, the Cristero war must be recognized as a tragic part (one among
others) of the process of formation of our Nation, and also as an example of
the high cost that political struggles between the summits of power can have
for society when they act irresponsibly.
